{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-tn","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"0b02b7e642693d958f9aeb1f4cd2b3243ac07d0955b1b2c7d286cceb1e29a0da","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-tn-class-d:lineage:105","source_registry_sha256":"8b0b6a068a0aa720d419171b5007a2610ed6c5012eeff522b57713cf9226eb71","source_liveness_sha256":"d27b9a94f03ec29d960b8eea38966606a7d3fdb703ad30b19ecd93f9bc70d0c7"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Special driving conditions and your vehicle","heading":"C — Special driving conditions and your vehicle: avoiding collisions by stopping, turning or speeding up, antilock and standard brakes, evasive steering, animal and deer crashes, the causes of crashes, driver fitness, vehicle maintenance and road and traffic conditions","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Special driving conditions and your vehicle: avoiding collisions by stopping, turning or speeding up, antilock and standard brakes, evasive steering, animal and deer crashes, the causes of crashes, driver fitness, vehicle maintenance and road and traffic conditions
Knowledge domain: how to get out of trouble and keep your car ready for it — the three ways to avoid a collision, how to brake hard with and without antilock brakes, how to hold the wheel and steer around a hazard, how to avoid and handle animal crashes, what really causes crashes, how vision, fatigue, health and emotions affect your fitness to drive, which vehicle systems to check, and how road and traffic conditions change the way you drive.

FACT_ID: sec15-F01 | anchor: A01
Most crashes happen in clear weather rather than in snow, rain or fog, so a pleasant day can be just as deadly. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0110]

FACT_ID: sec15-F02 | anchor: A01
When a collision seems about to happen, many drivers panic and do nothing, yet there is almost always some action that can avoid the crash or lessen it. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0110]

FACT_ID: sec15-F03 | anchor: A01
To avoid a collision a driver has three options: stop, turn, or speed up. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0110]

FACT_ID: sec15-F04 | anchor: A01
To stop quickly with antilock brakes, press the brake pedal as hard as you can and keep firm pressure on it, without letting up even when the pedal pushes back. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0110]

FACT_ID: sec15-F05 | anchor: A01
To stop quickly without antilock brakes, brake as hard as you can without locking the wheels, since braking too hard or too long can cause a skid. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0110]

FACT_ID: sec15-F06 | anchor: A01
Without antilock brakes, if the wheels lock and you feel a skid, let up on the pedal quickly, then press down again once the skid stops, repeating until the car stops. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0110]

FACT_ID: sec15-F07 | anchor: A01
In an emergency with antilock brakes the wheels do not lock and the car can still be steered, while without them all wheels may lock and the skidding car cannot be steered properly. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0110]

FACT_ID: sec15-F08 | anchor: A01
In most cases you can turn your vehicle faster than you can stop it, so if you cannot stop in time, steer around the hazard and brake only if you must. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0110]

FACT_ID: sec15-F09 | anchor: A01
For quick turns, grip the wheel with both hands on opposite sides at about the 9 o'clock and 3 o'clock positions, which also keeps your wrists and forearms out of the air bag's main impact area. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0110]

FACT_ID: sec15-F10 | anchor: A02
After steering away from a hazard, be ready to keep control and steer where you want the car to go, because some drivers dodge one crash only to cause another. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0111]

FACT_ID: sec15-F11 | anchor: A02
With antilock brakes you can steer while braking without skidding, which helps when you must swerve and stop or slow quickly. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0111]

FACT_ID: sec15-F12 | anchor: A02
Without antilock brakes, to turn quickly you must let up on the brake pedal and then turn the wheel. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0111]

FACT_ID: sec15-F13 | anchor: A02
Stop braking if you feel the front wheels lock, and do not turn so sharply that the car can only plow straight ahead. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0111]

FACT_ID: sec15-F14 | anchor: A02
It is generally better to drive off the road than to crash head-on into another vehicle. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0111]

FACT_ID: sec15-F15 | anchor: A02
Speeding up can be the right move when another vehicle is about to hit you from the side or behind and there is room ahead, but slow down once the danger passes. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0111]

FACT_ID: sec15-F16 | anchor: A02
Fall is the peak season for deer crashes, because autumn's mating and hunting seasons make deer more active and likely to wander. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0111]

FACT_ID: sec15-F17 | anchor: A02
Crashes with deer are generally the most dangerous and costly kind of animal crash. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0111]

FACT_ID: sec15-F18 | anchor: A02
Be especially alert for deer at dusk and dawn, when they come out to feed, and near woods and water. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0111]

FACT_ID: sec15-F19 | anchor: A02
If you see one deer, expect that several others may be close by. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0111]

FACT_ID: sec15-F20 | anchor: A02
If hitting an animal seems unavoidable, do not swerve, since swerving may raise your risk of injury; keep the car under control and on the road. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0111]

FACT_ID: sec15-F21 | anchor: A02
Report a crash with a large animal such as a deer or farm animal to the police. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0111]

FACT_ID: sec15-F22 | anchor: A02
Never pump the brake pedal in a car with antilock brakes, even when the pedal pulses; the pulsing is the system pumping the brakes faster than you could. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0111]

FACT_ID: sec15-F23 | anchor: A03
Do not freeze at the wheel or jerk it suddenly in an emergency, because a jerk can send you into another object or off the road and into a rollover. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0112]

FACT_ID: sec15-F24 | anchor: A03
Never drive a car with antilock brakes more aggressively than one without them. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0112]

FACT_ID: sec15-F25 | anchor: A03
Human error is the single most common cause of traffic crashes, and the leading factors are excessive speed, lack of concentration and improper evasive action. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0112]

FACT_ID: sec15-F26 | anchor: A03
Safe driving depends on three parts of the highway system, the driver, the vehicle and the road, and neglecting any of them contributes to most crashes. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0112]

FACT_ID: sec15-F27 | anchor: A03
Temporary conditions such as anger, worry, frustration, fatigue or even a cold can make you an unsafe driver. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0112]

FACT_ID: sec15-F28 | anchor: A04
Because seeing well is so important, have your eyes checked by an eye specialist every year or two. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0113]

FACT_ID: sec15-F29 | anchor: A04
If your license shows the corrective lens restriction, code 01, you must wear your glasses or contacts at all times while driving, or you could be ticketed and fined. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0113]

FACT_ID: sec15-F30 | anchor: A04
Do not wear dark sunglasses or tinted contact lenses at night, since they cut the light you need to see. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0113]

FACT_ID: sec15-F31 | anchor: A04
On long drives, stop for a break every hour or more often if needed, walking around and getting fresh air and a drink. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0113]

FACT_ID: sec15-F32 | anchor: A04
Never drive while sleepy; pulling over for a few hours of sleep beats gambling that you can stay awake. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0113]

FACT_ID: sec15-F33 | anchor: A04
In Tennessee, a person with epilepsy may drive if under a doctor's care and seizure-free for at least six months. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0113]

FACT_ID: sec15-F34 | anchor: A04
If you are angry or excited, give yourself time to calm down before driving, and if you are impatient, plan extra time for trips so delays do not tempt you to speed. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0113]

FACT_ID: sec15-F35 | anchor: A05
Worn or bald tires lengthen stopping distance, make turning harder on wet roads, raise the chance of a flat and can cause hydroplaning. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0114]

FACT_ID: sec15-F36 | anchor: A05
In the penny test, insert a penny head first into the tread; if the tread does not reach Lincoln's head, 2/32 inch, the tire is illegal and unsafe and must be replaced. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0114]

FACT_ID: sec15-F37 | anchor: A05
Use the recommended tire pressure on the sticker in the driver's door jamb, not the pressure printed on the tire, which is only the tire's maximum. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0114]

FACT_ID: sec15-F38 | anchor: A06
Never turn the ignition to the lock position while the car is moving, because the steering wheel will lock and you will lose control [A06] [A05].
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0115]

FACT_ID: sec15-F39 | anchor: A06
A sleepy feeling while driving or riding may mean an exhaust leak, which must be fixed at once because exhaust gases can kill inside a vehicle in a very short time. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0115]

FACT_ID: sec15-F40 | anchor: A06
Never run the engine in a closed garage or wherever the tailpipe may be blocked, including when the car is stuck in mud or snow. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0115]

FACT_ID: sec15-F41 | anchor: A06
Make sure your vehicle has at least a half tank of gas before any trip of significant length. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0115]

FACT_ID: sec15-F42 | anchor: A07
Near schools, playgrounds and residential streets, always watch for children who may cross, run or ride into the street without looking. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0116]

Misconceptions: bad weather is not when most crashes happen; antilock brakes are not pumped; swerving hard to miss a deer is often more dangerous than hitting it; antilock brakes do not make aggressive driving safe; the pressure on the tire sidewall is a maximum, not the recommended pressure; a sleepy feeling in the car can be an exhaust leak, not just tiredness.
Mnemonics: stop, turn or speed up; stomp and steer, never pump, with antilock brakes; nine and three on the wheel; driver, vehicle, road; penny to Lincoln's head.
Glossary: antilock brakes means a system that keeps wheels from locking so you can steer while braking; evasive steering means turning to go around a hazard; peripheral vision means seeing out of the corners of your eyes; carbon monoxide means the deadly gas in engine exhaust.
Dynamic facts: the epilepsy seizure-free period, the corrective lens restriction code and the legal tread depth are set by Tennessee rules and can change; confirm them on official Tennessee sources before showing them to learners.
